summary: A Live Science article explains how a UN-backed global program aims to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 using existing treatment and prevention tools. Progress is real, but 2022 data show the world is off target, especially for children, young women, key populations, and people who can't afford new drugs like cabotegravir. Experts say access, not science, is the main barrier, and that a vaccine and cure remain worth pursuing.
one_line: Experts say existing HIV drugs and prevention tools could end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 if access gaps are closed.
key_facts: In 2022 there were 1.3 million new HIV infections and around half that many deaths worldwide.
If the UN program succeeds, 2030 would see 200,000 new HIV infections and 130,000 AIDS-related deaths, 90% fewer than in 2010.
The first HIV treatment, AZT (azidothymidine), was approved in 1987; powerful treatments have existed since 1996.
The 95-95-95 target for 2025 means 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of those diagnosed take HIV drugs, and 95% of those treated are virally suppressed (about 86% of all people with HIV).
In 2022, only 76% of the 39 million people with HIV worldwide were taking ART and 71% were virally suppressed.
In 2022, only 57% of the 1.5 million children under 15 with HIV received treatment, 46% were virally suppressed, and an estimated 84,000 died of AIDS-related illnesses.
Nearly 1 in 6 new HIV cases in 2022 were in girls and women ages 15 to 24, many in sub-Saharan Africa.
Cabotegravir (Apretude), a bimonthly injectable PrEP, costs $3,700 per dose in the U.S.; its nonprofit price will be around $30 a dose, and no cabotegravir is yet available in Africa.
About 44% of transgender people with HIV are on ART, versus 78% of men who have sex with men, 65% of sex workers and 69% of people who inject drugs.
An estimated 25% of people stop ART, sometimes for six months or more, often due to stigma, clinic access, or cost.
Botswana, Eswatini, Rwanda, Tanzania and Zimbabwe have already hit the 95-95-95 target, with 16 more countries close.
In the U.S. in 2021, 75% of diagnosed people received some HIV care and 66% were virally suppressed.
Eastern Europe and Central Asia lag, with just 51% of people with HIV getting ART.
About a quarter of people with HIV worldwide are at least 50 years old.
